Rumors about Apple developing a foldable clamshell device have been around for a long time — it could be an iPad, a Mac, both, or some hybrid of the two.

There were recent reports that, although this had been a priority project for incoming CEO John Ternus, the plan has been canceled — but I don't think that's entirely accurate…

Personally, I believe the Mac+iPad hybrid concept has essentially been overtaken by events. Today's Macs can run iPhone and iPad apps, and iPhone Mirroring is another tool that achieves much the same thing for many of us. We've also seen a growing convergence between the two operating systems, and I believe this trend will continue: we are now well past the stage that Apple once described as simply trying to force a toaster and a refrigerator together.

But I do think that, when the technology matures to the point where a software keyboard can truly replace a hardware one, we will eventually have an all-screen foldable Mac. That won't happen in the short term, but it will happen.

The dynamic keyboard transition

I think it's still a long way off, because I believe there will first be a transition phase involving dynamic hardware keyboards. I've been talking about why I believe this is the future for a full ten years now, and while such tech is used in specific niche applications today, it still hasn't gone mainstream.

The Sonder Keyboard was one of the early attempts, using tiny e-ink displays to redefine the labels and functions of the keys.

For example, for someone who spends all day editing video in Final Cut Pro, a QWERTY keyboard is virtually useless, which is why physical keyboards and keyboard covers have a market.

Wouldn't it be smarter if our MacBook keyboard or our desktop Magic Keyboard could automatically relabel itself depending on the app being used at the time?

A software keyboard with the feel of a hardware one

But the long-term goal is always going to be a full software keyboard. Back in 2016, I argued that the case Steve Jobs made for virtual buttons when introducing the iPhone applied equally to Mac keyboards.

Of course, there are three problems with a software keyboard:

  • Glass keyboards are uncomfortable to type on
  • We rely on key travel for feedback and comfort
  • Touch-typists need to be able to feel the position of a key before pressing it

Apple already has patented tech to address each of these in turn. First, using a flexible display rather than traditional glass would allow the surface to deform when a virtual key is pressed. The second issue can be addressed with this deformation combined with haptic motors. Finally, there are two approaches to the question of being able to feel physical keys with a finger.

Apple's patent uses electrostatic charges to make the user feel a change in surface texture. In other words, it would apply a charge to the display surface to make it feel as though a physical button were present, even though the surface remains flat. And in 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University came up with an alternative approach.

It's a question of when, not if

Of course, all of this is still at a very early stage, but we only have to look at the precedent of the Mac trackpad. These sound and feel like mechanical devices, but for many years they have in fact been solid-state devices that simulate physical clicks through haptic technology — and they are extremely convincing.

A software keyboard will eventually reach the same level of maturity. Whether it's the approach currently proposed by Apple, or new technologies that haven't yet appeared, all three problems will be solved.

At that point, Steve's argument will apply equally to the Mac. In clamshell mode, the keyboard will automatically reconfigure itself into whatever layout best suits the task being performed. And when we just want one giant screen, whether for watching a movie or drawing with an Apple Pencil, we simply unfold it to double the screen size.

So I'm entirely open to the idea that the first-generation model may have been put on hold for now, but that's absolutely not the same as saying it's been canceled. The technology's time will come.

Those are my thoughts — what are yours? Please share them in the comments.
